citation: Wang Z, Tang Y, Wang G, Deng Y, Jiang Y, Sun W, Sun X, Ip P. Insufficient Sleep is Associated With Increasing Trends in Adolescent Suicidal Behaviors. J Adolesc Health. 2024 Jun;74(6):1198-1207.
your_quote: Multivariate logistic regression showed that adolescents with insufficient sleep were more likely to report suicidal ideation (aOR=1.38[95%CI: 1.28, 1.48], p<0.001), suicide plan (aOR=1.34[95%CI: 1.23, 1.46], p<0.001), and suicide attempts(aOR=1.24[95%CI: 1.17, 1.38], p<0.001) than those with sufficient sleep (Figure 1).
your_note: Source: PMC11137680 (accepted manuscript full text) + PubMed abstract. Adjusted OR for suicide plan, insufficient vs sufficient sleep = 1.34 (1.23, 1.46). log OR = ln(1.34) = 0.292670. SE = (ln(1.46)-ln(1.23))/3.92 = (0.378436-0.207014)/3.92 = 0.171422/3.92 = 0.043730. Exposure contrast in the paper is DICHOTOMOUS: 'Responses were dichotomized into insufficient sleep (<8h) and sufficient sleep (>=8h)'. The target's dose 7.0 h / referent 8.5 h are plausible category midpoints for that dichotomy but are not values the paper reports, so the dose/referent fields are an imputation by the task spec rather than an exact match. n = 73,356 pooled YRBS 2007-2019 respondents (the paper does not give a separate analytic n for this model). Model adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, depressive symptoms, overweight, cigarette/alcohol/marijuana/illicit drug use and survey year. Design is repeated cross-sectional national survey -> cross_sectional / TX; RoB high (self-reported exposure and outcome, cross-sectional, plausible reverse causation).

citation: Ferrie JE, Shipley MJ, Cappuccio FP, Brunner E, Miller MA, Kumari M, Marmot MG. A prospective study of change in sleep duration: associations with mortality in the Whitehall II cohort. Sleep. 2007 Dec;30(12):1659-1666.
your_quote: Non-CVD | Number of deaths | 38 |  | 33 | 45 | Hazard ratio (95% CI) - Fully adjusted # | 0.98 (0.62-1.57) | 1.0 | 1.44 (0.95-2.18) | 2.06 (1.38-3.08)  [Table 4, column 'Increase from 7 or 8 hours']
your_note: Source: PMC2276139 full text. Table 4 'Mortality from Phase 3 Onwards by Change in the Number of Hours Sleep Between Phase 1 and Phase 3', Non-CVD row, column 'Increase from 7 or 8 hours'. I took the FULLY ADJUSTED HR = 2.06 (1.38-3.08); log HR = ln(2.06) = 0.722706, SE = (ln(3.08)-ln(1.38))/3.92 = (1.124660-0.322084)/3.92 = 0.802577/3.92 = 0.204808. AMBIGUITY: the age-adjusted HR is 2.09 (1.40-3.12) -> log HR 0.737164, SE 0.204429, and that is the number highlighted in the abstract ('hazard ratio 2.1 (1.4-3.1)'). I chose the maximally adjusted estimate per standard synthesis practice; Cappuccio et al. 2010 also cite 2.06 (1.38-3.08) for this estimate. The two differ trivially (0.723 vs 0.737 on the log scale). SIGN: the exposure here is an INCREASE in sleep (from a habitual 7 or 8 h), not short sleep, so the positive value means elevated non-CVD mortality with sleep EXTENSION; the batch convention 'positive = elevated risk with short sleep' does not apply to this construct. n = 7,729 is the analytic sample for the change-in-sleep analyses overall ('7729 of the same participants were included in the analyses at Phase 3 and the analyses of change in sleep duration'); the paper does not report the subgroup n for this contrast, only 45 non-CVD deaths in the 'increase from 7 or 8 hours' group and 76 deaths in its referent (no change) group. Phase 1 to Phase 3 gap is 5-6 years, consistent with target 2190 days. RoB high for this specific estimate: reverse causation is a major and author-acknowledged threat (the authors speculate about undiagnosed disease / cancer-related fatigue driving the sleep increase).

citation: Daghlas I, Dashti HS, Lane J, Aragam KG, Rutter MK, Saxena R, Vetter C. Sleep Duration and Myocardial Infarction. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2019 Sep 10;74(10):1304-1314.
your_quote: IVW estimates in two-sample MR were consistent with a causal effect of short sleep duration on MI (ORper additional h of sleep= 0.80, 0.67-0.95, p=0.013; ORshort sleep = 1.19, 1.09-1.29, p=4.2e-04; Figure 3).
your_note: Source: PMC6785011 full text. Two-sample IVW MR of CONTINUOUS genetically predicted sleep duration against MI in CARDIoGRAMplusC4D: OR = 0.80 (0.67-0.95) PER ADDITIONAL HOUR of sleep. ln(0.80) = -0.223144. SIGN/UNIT CONFLICT IN THE TARGET SPEC (flagged): target_unit says 'per +1 h genetically predicted sleep' (which would give -0.223144), but target_exposure_type says 'per_hour_less_sleep' and the batch sign convention requires POSITIVE = elevated risk with short sleep. I followed the exposure_type + sign convention and report +0.223144 = ln(1/0.80) = ln(1.25), i.e. per one hour LESS genetically predicted sleep. If the first team followed target_unit literally they will have -0.223144; the magnitude is identical. SE = (ln(0.95)-ln(0.67))/3.92 = (-0.051293+0.400478)/3.92 = 0.349184/3.92 = 0.089078 (unchanged by the sign flip). n = 43,676 cases + 128,199 controls = 171,875 (CARDIoGRAMplusC4D, no overlap with UK Biobank). Do NOT confuse with the binary short-sleep MR estimate in the abstract (OR 1.19, 1.09-1.29) or the one-sample UKB continuous estimate (OR 0.86, 0.70-1.06). RoB moderate: the sleep-duration instrument is associated with BMI (possible pleiotropy or mediation), though a BMI-adjusted instrument gave a similar result (OR 0.81, 0.65-0.99).

citation: Zhou Q, Zhang M, Hu D. Dose-response association between sleep duration and obesity risk: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies. Sleep and Breathing. 2019;23(4):1035-1045.
your_quote: Compared with 7-h sleep duration per day, the pooled relative risks for obesity were 1.09 (95% CI 1.05-1.14) for each 1-h decrement among individuals who slept < 7 h per day and 1.02 (95% CI 0.99-1.05) for each 1-h increment of sleep duration among individuals with longer sleep duration.
your_note: Source: PubMed abstract (PMID 30941582); full text paywalled (not in PMC, not open access per Unpaywall), so I could not read the body. The abstract states the target quantity unambiguously: RR 1.09 (1.05-1.14) per 1-h DECREMENT below 7 h, referent 7 h, which matches target dose 6.0 h vs referent 7.0 h exactly (one hour below the referent). log RR = ln(1.09) = 0.086178. SE = (ln(1.14)-ln(1.05))/3.92 = (0.131028-0.048790)/3.92 = 0.082238/3.92 = 0.020979. Sign is positive = elevated obesity risk with shorter sleep, consistent with the batch convention. n = null: the abstract reports '12 studies (16 reports)' but no pooled participant count, and I could not access the full text to obtain it. RoB moderate: pooled prospective cohorts with (predominantly) self-reported sleep duration.

citation: Fjell AM, Sorensen O, Wang Y, Amlien IK, Baare WFC, Bartres-Faz D, Boraxbekk C-J, Brandmaier AM, Demuth I, Drevon CA, Ebmeier KP, Ghisletta P, Kievit R, Kuhn S, Madsen KS, Mowinckel AM, Nyberg L, Sexton CE, Solé-Padullés C, Vidal-Pineiro D, Wagner G, Watne LO, Zsoldos E, Walhovd KB. Is Short Sleep Bad for the Brain? Brain Structure and Cognitive Function in Short Sleepers. The Journal of Neuroscience. 2023;43(28):5241-5250.
your_quote: Both group 1: Short sleep and no sleep problems/sleepiness (estimate = -0.16 SD, t = -3.80, p < 0.0002) and group 2: Short sleep and sleep problems/sleepiness (estimate = -0.19 SD, t = -9.94, p < 2.97e-09) showed significantly lower scores than group 3: Recommended sleep and no sleep problems/sleepiness.
your_note: Source: PMC10342221 full text. The paper reports general cognitive ability (GCA, a per-sample g-factor) in SD units, so the estimate is already a standardised mean difference; with these sample sizes Hedges' g == the reported d to 3 decimals. I chose the contrast that isolates sleep DURATION: group 1 (short sleep <=6 h, no sleep problems/sleepiness) vs group 3 (recommended 7-8 h, no sleep problems/sleepiness) = -0.16 SD. This matches target dose 6.0 h vs referent 7.5 h (<=6 h vs 7-8 h). AMBIGUITY: the other short-sleeper group (group 2, short sleep WITH sleep problems/sleepiness) vs group 3 is -0.19 SD; the abstract quotes '0.16 and 0.19 SDs' for the two short-sleeper groups and the paper reports no pooled short-sleep-vs-recommended estimate. If the first team pooled or picked group 2, expect -0.19 (SE 0.19/9.94 = 0.019). SE derived from the reported t: SE = |estimate|/|t| = 0.16/3.80 = 0.042105. n = 8,694 = the total GCA analytic sample across the four sleep groups ('General cognitive function (GCA) scores were available for 8694 of the classified participants'); the group-1-vs-group-3 subsample size is NOT reported (group 1 n = 740 and group 3 n = 3,886 in the full classified sample; the GCA subsample splits are only given as 2,173 for groups 1+2 and 6,521 for groups 3+4). Sign negative = worse cognition under short sleep, consistent with the batch convention. Design is a cross-sectional group comparison on self-reported sleep -> cross_sectional / TX; RoB high (cross-sectional, self-reported exposure, causality explicitly undetermined by the authors).

citation: You J, Guo Y, Wang YJ, Zhang Y, Wang HF, Wang LB, Kang JJ, Feng JF, Yu JT, Cheng W. Clinical trajectories preceding incident dementia up to 15 years before diagnosis: a large prospective cohort study. Molecular Psychiatry. 2024 Oct;29(10):3097-3105.
your_quote: Inadequate activity (3-5 year, overall time of activity, OR 0.82 [0.73-0.92]), drowsiness (3-5 year, sleep duration, OR 1.13 [1.04-1.24]) and weight loss (0-5 year, weight, OR 0.9 [0.83-0.98]) only exhibited associations within five years before the diagnosis.
your_note: Source: PubMed abstract (PMID 38678085) and the nature.com abstract page; full text is paywalled (not in PMC), so I could not verify the model from the body or the figures. OR 1.13 (1.04-1.24) for sleep duration in the 3-5-year pre-diagnosis window. log OR = ln(1.13) = 0.122218; SE = (ln(1.24)-ln(1.04))/3.92 = (0.215111-0.039221)/3.92 = 0.175891/3.92 = 0.044870. DIRECTION (flagged): the abstract labels this finding 'drowsiness', i.e. the OR is for LONGER sleep duration being associated with higher odds of dementia diagnosis 3-5 years later. I report it as the paper reports it (+0.122). Under the batch convention 'positive = elevated risk with short sleep' the sign would have to be flipped to -0.122. target_exposure_type is 'other', so the convention arguably does not bind here. n = null: the analysis is a matched case-control nested in UK Biobank (7,620 incident dementia cases, each matched to 10 controls) analysed in consecutive pre-diagnosis timeframes; the abstract does not give the analytic n for the 3-5-year window and I could not reach the full text. RoB high: this is by design a prodromal / reverse-causation analysis (the exposure is measured as a pre-diagnostic marker), so it cannot support a causal short-sleep-to-dementia interpretation.

citation: Depner CM, Melanson EL, Eckel RH, Snell-Bergeon JK, Perreault L, Bergman BC, Higgins JA, Guerin MK, Stothard ER, Morton SJ, Wright KP Jr. Ad libitum Weekend Recovery Sleep Fails to Prevent Metabolic Dysregulation during a Repeating Pattern of Insufficient Sleep and Weekend Recovery Sleep. Current Biology. 2019;29(6):957-967.e4.
your_quote: In the SR and WR groups, body weight was increased to a similar extent (SR versus WR P = 0.91; study day 13 versus baseline all P < 0.05) 1.4 +/- 0.5kg and 1.3 +/- 0.4kg, respectively, on the morning of study day 13 versus baseline (Figure S2E).
your_note: Source: PMC12798825 full text. I report the SR arm (5-h sleep opportunity, 9 nights of insufficient sleep, no weekend recovery): body weight +1.4 kg on the morning of study day 13 vs baseline, n = 14. The +/- 0.5 is a standard error, not an SD: for the CON arm (1.0 +/- 0.8 kg, n = 8) treating 0.8 as SE gives t = 1.25, two-sided p = 0.25, matching the reported P = 0.23, whereas treating it as an SD would give p = 0.008, inconsistent with the reported P. So your_se = 0.5. AMBIGUITY (flagged): the target names dose 5.0 h vs referent 9.0 h, which implies the SR-vs-CON between-arm contrast = 1.4 - 1.0 = 0.4 kg; but the construct name is 'body_weight_change_kg_sleep_restriction' and the paper only reports WITHIN-arm changes from baseline, with no formal CON-vs-SR test of weight change. I report the within-arm 1.4 kg. Note that the 9-h control arm also gained 1.0 +/- 0.8 kg (P = 0.23) because food was ad libitum and ~33% more calories were presented than at baseline, so the within-arm 1.4 kg overstates the sleep-restriction effect. Design: randomised three-arm in-laboratory protocol (rct_parallel), but the extracted number is a within-group pre-post change; either way tier T1. RoB some_concerns (small n, no blinding possible, confounding of the pre-post change by the ad libitum feeding regimen as shown by the control arm).

citation: Evans MA, Buysse DJ, Marsland AL, Wright AGC, Foust J, Carroll LW, Kohli N, Mehra R, Jasper A, Srinivasan S, Hall MH. Meta-analysis of age and actigraphy-assessed sleep characteristics across the lifespan. Sleep. 2021;44(9):zsab088.
your_quote: This meta-analysis included 53 articles with 58 effect sizes and 11 525 participants. The overall effect size was r = -0.05, 95% CI [-0.10, -0.001], p = .05, T2 = 0.02, I2 = 42.24% (Figure 4), indicating a small correlation between older age and lower sleep efficiency.
your_note: Source: PMC8436145 full text. Pooled age-sleep-efficiency correlation r = -0.05, 95% CI [-0.10, -0.001]. SE on the r scale = (-0.001 - (-0.10))/3.92 = 0.099/3.92 = 0.025255. Caveat: the meta-analysis was performed on Fisher's z and back-transformed to r, so an SE computed from the back-transformed CI is approximate; the equivalent SE on the Fisher-z scale would be marginally larger. n = 11,525 participants (53 articles, 58 effect sizes). This analysis genuinely spans the lifespan (study mean ages 6.5-91.9 y); only the bedtime and wake-time meta-analyses were split at age 21/22, so 'across_lifespan' in the target construct is correct for sleep efficiency. RoB high: the authors judged the quality of evidence for sleep efficiency 'insufficient', the association was p = .05, and 'Removal of any one of 31 published effect sizes included in the meta-analysis rendered the overall association nonsignificant'. Descriptive/exposure-measurement quantity -> tier TX.

citation: Katz ES, Moore RH, Rosen CL, Mitchell RB, Amin R, Arens R, Muzumdar H, Chervin RD, Marcus CL, Paruthi S, Willging P, Redline S. Growth after adenotonsillectomy for obstructive sleep apnea: an RCT. Pediatrics. 2014;134(2):282-289.
your_quote: Interval increases in the BMI z score (0.13 vs. 0.31) was observed in both the WWSC and eAT intervention arms, respectively, but were greater with eAT (P < .0001).
your_note: Source: PMC4187239 full text (Childhood Adenotonsillectomy Trial growth paper). Value = between-arm difference in 7-month BMI z-score change, early adenotonsillectomy minus watchful waiting = 0.31 - 0.13 = 0.18 BMI z-score units. Table 3 corroborates: eAT BMI z 0.87 -> 1.18 (change 0.31); WWSC 0.87 -> 1.00 (change 0.13). SE derived from the Table 3 p-value for 'Interval change between groups' for BMI z score, unadjusted P = .004: z = 2.8782 (two-sided), SE = 0.18/2.8782 = 0.062539. (Adjusted P values were .003 and .003, giving essentially the same SE.) INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY IN THE PAPER (flagged): the abstract states P < .0001 for the between-arm difference in BMI z-score change, whereas Table 3 gives P = .004/.003; I used the table. n = 396 (204 eAT + 192 WWSC with anthropometry at both visits), out of 464 randomised. Sign: positive = greater BMI z-score gain after adenotonsillectomy (i.e. after OSA treatment / sleep improvement). RoB some_concerns: rigorous multicentre RCT with objective anthropometry, but ~15% of randomised children lack anthropometry at follow-up and growth was a secondary outcome. Exposure is OSA treatment, not sleep duration.

citation: Akerstedt T, Ghilotti F, Grotta A, Zhao H, Adami HO, Trolle-Lagerros Y, Bellocco R. Sleep duration and mortality - Does weekend sleep matter? Journal of Sleep Research. 2019;28(1):e12712.
your_quote: The weekday and weekend sleep duration analysis shows that for age <65 years group sleeping 5 hr or less, both during weekdays and weekend (SS), was associated with a 65% higher mortality rate (HR 1.65; 95% CI 1.22-2.23) compared with those consistently sleeping 6 or 7 hr per night (Figure 4).
your_note: Source: PMC7003477 full text (Swedish National March Cohort). Consistently short sleep (<=5 h on both weekdays and weekends) vs consistently 6-7 h, among participants aged <65 y at enrolment: HR 1.65 (1.22-2.23). This matches target dose 5.0 h and referent 6.5 h (midpoint of the 6-7 h referent category) exactly. log HR = ln(1.65) = 0.500775. SE = (ln(2.23)-ln(1.22))/3.92 = (0.802002-0.198851)/3.92 = 0.603151/3.92 = 0.153865. Adjusted for sex, BMI, smoking, alcohol, education, physical activity, shift work and Charlson index. n = null: the estimate is for the <65 y stratum only and the paper does not report that stratum's sample size. For context, the full cohort is 43,880; the six weekday/weekend sleep groups in Table 1 sum to 38,015; the short-short group is 1,592 across all ages with 323 deaths. Sensitivity analysis excluding the first 2 years of follow-up gave HR 1.56 (1.13-2.15). RoB moderate: large well-adjusted prospective cohort but self-reported sleep and the proportional hazards assumption was violated when age groups were pooled.

citation: Groen JA, Pabilonia SW. Snooze or lose: High school start times and academic achievement. Economics of Education Review. 2019;72:204-218.
target_unit: hours of nighttime sleep per hour later start time
your_quote: For female students, we find that in response to a delay in start time of one hour, they sleep 0.599 hours (36 minutes) more per night and 0.634 hours (38 minutes) more on their diary day.
your_note: SOURCE CAVEAT (flagged): the published Economics of Education Review 2019 article is paywalled and I could not obtain it. I extracted from the IZA Discussion Paper 11166 (2017) working-paper version of the same study (https://docs.iza.org/dp11166.pdf), Table 6 'Effects of School Start Time on Sleep', Panel 1 (Females), column 'Nighttime diary sleep (M-TH)': coefficient on school start time = 0.599, clustered SE = 0.230 (in parentheses), *** p<0.01, 450 observations. The authors' own Monthly Labor Review summary of the PUBLISHED paper states females sleep '36 minutes more per school night for a 1-hour later start time' = 0.60 h, so the published coefficient is numerically equivalent; the published SE may differ slightly. SEX NOT SPECIFIED IN THE TARGET (flagged): the paper estimates separately by sex and only the female model is used as the first stage of the sleep -> reading-score IV model, so I used the female estimate. The male nighttime-sleep coefficient in this version is 0.327 (SE 0.228, not significant); note the published abstract describes males as also getting more nighttime sleep, so working-paper and published versions differ for males. PSID-CDS time diaries; identification is cross-school variation in start times with controls for day length, lagged test scores and school/district/county/state characteristics, used as an instrument for sleep -> coded instrumental_variable / T2 (quasi_experiment would also map to T2). RoB moderate: non-randomised start-time variation, residual confounding possible, modest n.

citation: Prather AA, Leung CW. Association of insufficient sleep with respiratory infection among adults in the United States. JAMA Internal Medicine. 2016;176(6):850-852.
your_quote: Infectionsc | Sleep duration, h | <=5 | 188 (5.9) | 1.82 (1.42-2.34) | <.001 | 1.51 (1.18-1.93) | .001   [Table: Self-reported Sleep and Rates of Colds and Infections; footnote c: Infections include influenza, pneumonia, and ear infection]
your_note: Source: PMC4899278 full text (research letter, no structured abstract in PubMed). Outcome = self-reported infection (influenza, pneumonia or ear infection) in the past 30 days; exposure <=5 h vs 7-8 h referent, matching target dose 5 h / referent 7.5 h. I used MODEL 2 (fully adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, household income, marital status, smoking, physical activity, BMI and survey year): OR 1.51 (1.18-1.93). log OR = ln(1.51) = 0.412110; SE = (ln(1.93)-ln(1.18))/3.92 = (0.657520-0.165514)/3.92 = 0.492006/3.92 = 0.125512. AMBIGUITY: Model 1 (age and sex only) gives OR 1.82 (1.42-2.34) -> log OR 0.598837, SE 0.127422, and that is the number quoted in the paper's Results text; if the first team extracted the text rather than the fully adjusted column they will have 0.599. n = 22,726 NHANES 2005-2012 participants (the letter gives no separate analytic n; 851 infection cases across the four sleep categories). RoB high: cross-sectional, both exposure and outcome self-reported; the authors state 'The cross-sectional nature of the data in our study precludes any causal inferences'.

citation: Svensson T, Saito E, Svensson AK, Melander O, Orho-Melander M, Mimura M, Rahman S, Sawada N, Koh WP, Shu XO, Tsuji I, Kanemura S, Park SK, Nagata C, Tsugane S, Cai H, Yuan JM, Matsuyama S, Sugawara Y, Wada K, Yoo KY, Chia KS, Boffetta P, Ahsan H, Zheng W, Kang D, Potter JD, Inoue M. Association of Sleep Duration With All- and Major-Cause Mortality Among Adults in Japan, China, Singapore, and Korea. JAMA Netw Open. 2021 Sep 1;4(9):e2122837.
your_quote: The strongest associations between sleep duration and mortality for both men (HR, 1.43, 95% CI, 1.34-1.53) and women (HR, 1.55, 95% CI, 1.42-1.70) were found for participants with the longest sleep duration (>=10 hours). Multivariable adjustment only slightly attenuated these associations (men: HR, 1.34, 95% CI, 1.26-1.44; women: HR, 1.48, 95% CI, 1.36-1.61).
your_note: Source: PMC8417759 full text (Asia Cohort Consortium pooled analysis of 9 cohorts). All-cause mortality, women, >=10 h vs 7 h referent, MULTIVARIABLE adjusted: HR 1.48 (1.36-1.61). Matches target dose 10.0 h / referent 7.0 h. log HR = ln(1.48) = 0.392042; SE = (ln(1.61)-ln(1.36))/3.92 = (0.476234-0.307485)/3.92 = 0.168750/3.92 = 0.043048. The minimally adjusted estimate is HR 1.55 (1.42-1.70) -> log HR 0.438255, SE 0.045830, if the first team took that. n = 178,542 women (55.3% of 322,721 participants), 13,768 deaths among women. TARGET SPEC ERROR (flagged): target_exposure_type is 'recovery_sleep', but this is habitual self-reported LONG sleep duration at baseline, not recovery sleep. The outcome construct, dose, referent, sex and scale are all unambiguous, so the value is unaffected. RoB moderate: large pooled prospective cohorts with extensive adjustment, but self-reported sleep and the usual reverse-causation concern for long sleep (early deaths were not excluded).

citation: Sivertsen B, Harvey AG, Gradisar M, Pallesen S, Hysing M. Delayed sleep-wake phase disorder in young adults: prevalence and correlates from a national survey of Norwegian university students. Sleep Med. 2021;77:184-191.
your_quote: The overall prevalence of DSWPD was 3.3%, and significantly higher in male (4.7%) than female (2.7%) students.
your_note: Source: PubMed abstract (PMID 33097403). Full text is paywalled (Elsevier; not in PMC; the only green-OA copy is a JavaScript-only NVA repository landing page I could not retrieve), so the quote is from the abstract, which states the target quantity directly. Male DSWPD prevalence = 4.7% -> your_value = 0.047 as a proportion. n DERIVED, NOT REPORTED: the abstract gives 50,054 included students, 69.1% women, so males = 50,054 x (1 - 0.691) = 15,467. Other SHoT2018 papers quote 68.9% women, which would give 15,567, so the male denominator is approximate to about +/-100; the SE is insensitive to this. SE computed as a binomial SE for a proportion: sqrt(0.047 x 0.953 / 15467) = sqrt(2.895e-6) = 0.001702. This ignores the survey design and non-response weighting, and the paper reports no CI for the sex-specific prevalence. RoB high for a prevalence estimate: 30.8% response rate (50,054 of 162,512 invited) and DSWPD operationalised from self-report rather than clinical assessment, despite using ICSD-3 criteria.

citation: Lo JC, Ong JL, Leong RLF, Gooley JJ, Chee MWL. Cognitive Performance, Sleepiness, and Mood in Partially Sleep Deprived Adolescents: The Need for Sleep Study. Sleep. 2016;39(3):687-698.
your_quote: In terms of effect size, performance in the PVT was the most sensitive to partial sleep deprivation of all the tests in this study (f 2 = 1.48; Figure 3).
your_note: Source: PMC4763363 full text (Need for Sleep Study; 7 nights 5 h TIB vs 9 h TIB, parallel groups, boarding school). THE PAPER DOES NOT REPORT A HEDGES' g OR ANY GROUP MEANS/SDs FOR PVT LAPSES. It reports only (a) a group x day interaction F(9,456) = 9.09, P < 0.001, and (b) Cohen's local f2 = 1.48 for that interaction, computed from a PROC MIXED model over the restriction days with baseline performance as a covariate. CONVERSION (approximate, low confidence): f = sqrt(1.48) = 1.21655; assuming a balanced two-group contrast, d = 2f = 2.43311; Hedges' correction J = 1 - 3/(4*56-9) = 0.986047, so g = 2.39915, reported as -2.399 because more PVT lapses = worse performance under restriction (batch convention: negative = worse under restriction). SE(g) = sqrt((n1+n2)/(n1*n2) + g^2/(2(n1+n2-2))) = sqrt(56/(30*26) + 5.7559/108) = sqrt(0.071795 + 0.053287) = 0.354. CAVEAT: f2 here is a local effect size for a group x DAY INTERACTION across 8 days in a repeated-measures model, not a single-timepoint between-group standardised difference, so d = 2*sqrt(f2) is not strictly valid and the magnitude may be inflated. A first team that digitised Figure 2A or used a different conversion could differ substantially. Group sizes: SR n = 30, control n = 26, total 56. For scale, the paper notes 'an average of 18 lapses were found after 7 nights of 5 h TIB in the current study'. RoB some_concerns (randomised parallel groups but no blinding possible, small n, baseline group differences handled by covariate adjustment).

citation: Yin J, Jin X, Shan Z, Li S, Huang H, Li P, Peng X, Peng Z, Yu K, Bao W, Yang W, Chen X, Liu L. Relationship of Sleep Duration With All-Cause Mortality and Cardiovascular Events: A Systematic Review and Dose-Response Meta-Analysis of Prospective Cohort Studies. J Am Heart Assoc. 2017 Sep 9;6(9):e005947.
your_quote: Sleep Duration | All-Cause Mortality (n=40a) ... 5 h | 1.04 (1.03-1.05) ... 7 h | 1.00   [Table 2: Association Between Sleep Duration and All-Cause Mortality, Total CVD, CHD and Stroke From Non-Linear Dose-Response Analysis; footnote a: n denotes number of risk estimates]
your_note: Source: PMC5634263 full text. Table 2 gives RRs at selected sleep durations from the restricted-cubic-spline non-linear dose-response model with 7 h as referent; at 5 h, all-cause mortality RR = 1.04 (1.03-1.05). This is the exact match to target dose 5 h / referent 7 h. log RR = ln(1.04) = 0.039221; SE = (ln(1.05)-ln(1.03))/3.92 = (0.048790-0.029559)/3.92 = 0.019231/3.92 = 0.004906. AMBIGUITY (flagged): the abstract-level headline is instead the LINEAR trend 'RR 1.06 (1.04-1.07) per 1-hour reduction' below 7 h; compounded over the 2-hour gap from 7 h to 5 h that would give 1.06^2 = 1.1236, log RR = 2*ln(1.06) = 0.116538, SE approximately 2*(ln(1.07)-ln(1.04))/3.92 = 0.014266. So the first team may have either 0.0392 (spline value at 5 h, as I report) or roughly 0.0583 (single per-hour coefficient) or 0.1165 (compounded over 2 h). I chose the spline value because it is the only estimate that directly expresses 5 h vs 7 h. n = null: 40 risk estimates entered this non-linear analysis, but the paper does not report the corresponding participant total. Whole review: 67 articles, 3,582,016 participants, 241,107 all-cause deaths. RoB moderate: all included studies were prospective and mostly high NOS quality, but sleep duration was assessed by self-report questionnaire (48 studies) or interview (19 studies), and heterogeneity was moderate to high (I2 55.5%).

citation: Lowe CJ, Safati A, Hall PA. The neurocognitive consequences of sleep restriction: A meta-analytic review. Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews. 2017;80:586-604.
your_quote: This effect held for executive functioning (g=-0.324, p<0.001), sustained attention (g=-0.409, p<0.001), and long-term memory (g=-0.192, p=0.002).
your_note: Source: PubMed abstract (PMID 28757454). The full text is closed access (confirmed not OA via Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar), so I could not read the body or the domain-level table. The abstract reports the target quantity directly: long-term memory g = -0.192, p = 0.002. Already on the Hedges' g scale, negative = worse under sleep restriction, consistent with the batch convention. SE DERIVED FROM THE p-VALUE: for p = 0.002 two-sided, z = 3.0902, so SE = 0.192/3.0902 = 0.062132. This is an approximation because the reported p is rounded and the random-effects test may not be exactly normal; if the paper's table reports a CI the first team's SE may differ modestly. n = null: the abstract gives 61 studies from 71 populations for the OVERALL effect but no k or participant count for the long-term-memory subdomain. RoB some_concerns: meta-analysis of experimental sleep-restriction studies (hence tier T1), but the primary studies are small, typically unblinded lab protocols.

citation: Huang S, Deshpande A, Yeo SC, Lo JC, Chee MW, Gooley JJ. Sleep Restriction Impairs Vocabulary Learning when Adolescents Cram for Exams: The Need for Sleep Study. Sleep. 2016;39(9):1681-1690.
your_quote: The magnitude of the spacing effect was greater in students given 5 h of TIB versus 9 h of TIB (Spacing x TIB: LR chi 2 = 8.40, P < 0.01; See Table 2).
your_note: Source: PMC4989257 full text (Need for Sleep Study vocabulary-learning arm; 7 nights 5 h vs 9 h TIB, parallel groups). THE PAPER REPORTS NO HEDGES' g AND NO CELL MEANS/SDs for the Spacing x TIB interaction; Table 2 is supplied only as an image. The only statistic given for this interaction is a likelihood-ratio chi-square = 8.40 (1 df), P < 0.01. CONVERSION (approximate, low confidence): for 1 df, z = sqrt(8.40) = 2.89828. Treating the interaction as a between-group comparison of the within-subject spacing effect (spaced minus massed difference score), d = z * sqrt(1/n1 + 1/n2) = 2.89828 * sqrt(1/30 + 1/26) = 2.89828 * 0.267946 = 0.77658; Hedges' correction J = 1 - 3/(4*56-9) = 0.986047 gives g = 0.76574, reported as -0.766 because the interaction reflects a LARGER sleep-restriction penalty on massed items (worse recall under restriction), following the batch sign convention. SE(g) = sqrt(56/(30*26) + 0.5864/108) = sqrt(0.071795 + 0.005431) = 0.278. CAVEAT: the LR chi-square comes from a GLM pooling three retention-interval test sessions with several other factors, so the effective sample size exceeds 56 and this conversion is only approximate. Group sizes: 5-h TIB n = 30, 9-h TIB n = 26. Direction of the underlying finding: recall of massed items was significantly worse under restriction (Tukey P < 0.001) while spaced items did not differ (Tukey P = 0.80). RoB some_concerns.

citation: Swanson CM, Shea SA, Wolfe P, Cain SW, Munch M, Vujovic N, Czeisler CA, Buxton OM, Orwoll ES. Bone turnover markers after sleep restriction and circadian disruption: a mechanism for sleep-related bone loss in humans. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2017;102(10):3722-3730.
your_quote: CTX, ng/mL 0.92 +/- 0.13 | 0.03 +/- 0.02 (0.10)   [Table 1, 'Effect of Sleep Intervention ... Estimate +/- SEE (P Value)'; abbreviation SEE = standard error of estimate; N = 10]
your_note: Source: accepted-manuscript PDF via Monash repository plus PMC5630251. Table 1 and the abstract agree: 'There was no change in CTX (delta = 0.03 +/- 0.02 ng/mL, P = 0.10)'. your_value = +0.03 ng/mL (post-intervention minus baseline; positive = slightly higher bone resorption marker, i.e. directionally worse, but not statistically significant). your_se = 0.02, which Table 1 labels explicitly as SEE (standard error of estimate) from the mixed model for repeated measures, so no derivation was needed. n = 10 men (6 aged 20-27 y, 4 aged 55-65 y). TARGET SPEC MISMATCH (flagged): target_exposure_referent_h = 8, but the study's referent is the participants' BASELINE with a 10-h sleep opportunity ('light blue = baseline - 10 hours; purple = postintervention - approximately 5.6 hours'), so the true contrast is 5.6 h vs 10 h, not 5.6 h vs 8 h. Also, the exposure is NOT pure sleep restriction: sleep restriction to 5.6 h/24 h was imposed together with forced-desynchrony circadian disruption (recurring 28-hour day in dim light) for about 3 weeks, so sleep loss and circadian misalignment cannot be separated. RoB moderate: uncontrolled within-subject pre-post design, n = 10, all male, and the exposure is confounded by concurrent circadian disruption.

citation: Miller MA, Kruisbrink M, Wallace J, Ji C, Cappuccio FP. Sleep duration and incidence of obesity in infants, children, and adolescents: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective studies. Sleep. 2018;41(4):zsy018.
your_quote: Sleep duration was also associated with a significant change in BMI z-score (14 studies, 18 cohorts, 31665 participants; mean difference -0.03; -0.04 to -0.01 per hour sleep; p = .001) and in BMI (16 studies, 24 cohorts, 24894 participants; mean difference -0.03 kg/m2; -0.04 to -0.01 for every hour of increase in sleep; p = .001).
your_note: Source: PubMed abstract (PMID 29401314) verified against the full text in the Warwick WRAP open-access copy ('with a decrease in BMI per hour of increase in sleep (-0.03 [-0.04, -0.01])'). The target names BMI in kg/m2, so I used the BMI (not BMI z-score) pooled estimate: -0.03 kg/m2 (-0.04 to -0.01) per hour of increase in sleep, 16 studies, 24 cohorts, 24,894 participants. SE = (-0.01 - (-0.04))/3.92 = 0.03/3.92 = 0.007653. Note the CI is reported to only two decimal places, so this SE is coarse. SIGN: reported as -0.03 per hour MORE sleep, matching target_unit 'kg/m2 per hour of sleep'. If the intended parameterisation is per hour LESS sleep (target_exposure_type is 'per_hour_less_sleep'), the sign flips to +0.03. Do not confuse with the BMI z-score estimate, which is numerically also -0.03 but with n = 31,665 across 18 cohorts. Tier T5: meta-analysis of prospective paediatric cohorts with predominantly parent/self-reported sleep duration (some used actigraphy). RoB moderate (substantial heterogeneity, results presented by age strata).

citation: Pirie K, Peto R, Reeves GK, Green J, Beral V; Million Women Study Collaborators. The 21st century hazards of smoking and benefits of stopping: a prospective study of one million women in the UK. Lancet. 2013;381(9861):133-141.
your_quote: They also had slightly higher overall mortality, relative risk 1.05 (1.00-1.11), p=0.05.
your_note: Source: PMC3547248 full text (Million Women Study). Residual all-cause mortality among women who stopped smoking permanently at ages 25-34 years (mean 29), versus never-smokers: relative (rate) ratio 1.05 (1.00-1.11), p = 0.05. Corroborated in the abstract: 'Among ex-smokers who had stopped permanently at ages 25-34 years or at ages 35-44 years, the respective relative risks were 1.05 (95% CI 1.00-1.11) and 1.20 (1.14-1.26) for all-cause mortality'. log rate ratio = ln(1.05) = 0.048790. SE = (ln(1.11)-ln(1.00))/3.92 = 0.104360/3.92 = 0.026622. Because the lower limit is rounded to exactly 1.00, this SE is slightly conservative; deriving from p = 0.05 instead gives SE = 0.048790/1.95996 = 0.024893. This is Figure 4's 9-year relative risk measured from the 3-year postal resurvey onward, restricted to women who were ex-smokers at both recruitment and the resurvey and who stopped before age 55. n = null: the paper does not report the number of women in the stopped-at-25-34 category (only 86 observed lung cancer deaths vs about 46 expected). Whole cohort after exclusions: 1,180,652 women, 619,774 never-smokers (the reference group), 66,489 deaths. This is a comparator (smoking-cessation) benchmark, not a sleep exposure. RoB moderate: very large cohort with extensive adjustment (region, age, BMI, deprivation, alcohol, activity, height, oral contraceptives, menopausal status/HRT), self-reported smoking, and residual confounding/healthy-quitter selection remain possible.

citation: Cappuccio FP, D'Elia L, Strazzullo P, Miller MA. Sleep duration and all-cause mortality: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective studies. Sleep. 2010 May;33(5):585-592.
your_quote: In the pooled analysis, short duration of sleep (25 cohorts from 15 studies, n = 1,381,324 with 112,163 deaths) was associated with greater risk of death (RR: 1.12; 95% CI 1.06 to 1.18, P < 0.01), with no evidence of publication bias (P = 0.74; ...)
your_note: Source: PMC2864873 full text. Pooled RR for short sleep duration vs the reference category, all-cause mortality = 1.12 (1.06-1.18). log RR = ln(1.12) = 0.113329; SE = (ln(1.18)-ln(1.06))/3.92 = (0.165514-0.058269)/3.92 = 0.107246/3.92 = 0.027359. n = 1,381,324 participants in 25 cohorts from 15 studies, with 112,163 deaths (the short-sleep analysis specifically; the abstract's 1,382,999 / 112,566 figures cover all 16 studies / 27 cohorts including the long-sleep analysis). target_exposure_dose_h and target_exposure_referent_h are both null, which is appropriate: the review pooled heterogeneous category definitions - 'short sleepers (commonly < 7 h per night, often < 5 h per night)' vs 'those sleeping 7 to 8 h per night' - and the authors report that the estimate did not depend on whether short sleep was defined as <=5, <=6 or <=7 h. This is a categorical (not dose-response) meta-analysis, so design is coded meta_analysis_observational rather than dose_response_meta_analysis. Tier T5: prospective cohorts with sleep duration assessed by questionnaire. RoB moderate (significant heterogeneity, P = 0.02; no publication bias detected; adjustment varied across studies).

citation: Meininger JC, Gallagher MR, Eissa MA, Nguyen TQ, Chan W. Sleep duration and its association with ambulatory blood pressure in a school-based, diverse sample of adolescents. Am J Hypertens. 2014 Jul;27(7):948-955.
target_unit: mmHg per additional hour of nighttime sleep
your_quote: Sleep: night, hours | -0.57 | 0.14 | <0.0001 | -0.19 | 0.10 | 0.06   [Table 4. Mixed effects model for 24-hour ambulatory systolic and diastolic blood pressure in adolescents (n = 366); columns: Estimate, SE, P value for systolic then diastolic]
your_note: Source: PMC4118569 full text. Table 4, 'Sleep: night, hours' row, systolic blood pressure columns: estimate -0.57 mm Hg per additional hour of nighttime sleep, SE 0.14, P < 0.0001, from a mixed model for 24-hour ambulatory SBP. your_se = 0.14 is taken directly from the table; no derivation needed. n = 366 adolescents aged 11-16 y. Corroborated in the text: 'controlling for all covariables and sleep duration during the day, each additional hour of nighttime sleep was associated with lower SBP (-0.57mm Hg; P < 0.0001)'. Model controls for daytime sleep duration, BMI, physical activity, age, sex, ethnicity, sexual maturation, mother's education, and body position and location at each BP reading. SIGN: reported per ADDITIONAL hour of nighttime sleep, matching target_unit; if the intended parameterisation is per hour LESS sleep (target_exposure_type is 'per_hour_less_sleep'), the sign flips to +0.57. Do not confuse with the daytime-sleep (nap) coefficient of -0.73 mm Hg, or with the daytime-interval SBP model (-0.36 mm Hg per hour of nighttime sleep). Exposure was actigraphy-measured, but the design is explicitly cross-sectional ('This cross-sectional study tested the hypothesis...') -> tier TX, RoB high for causal inference.
